title: C#: the language (topics 01-14)
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 fund-cs-language row). Scope = Fundamentals C# topic gates 01-14. Sources = topic gate plus its first drill; siblings = other topic drills and related.json drills. Topics 06, 07, 08 and 10 have no row of their own on the binding list. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Assigning a struct copies it, assigning a class instance copies the reference so both names alias one object; putting a value type into object or an interface boxes it.
ideas.why: Mutating a struct copied out of a list changes nothing, mutating a shared class changes it everywhere, and boxing in hot loops allocates on every call.
ideas.prompt: `foreach (var c in counters) c.Reset();` works when Counter is a class but leaves the values unchanged when someone turns it into a struct. Explain, and say what you would do.
ideas.answer: With a class each element is a reference, so Reset changes the shared object. With a struct the loop variable is a copy, and the copy is reset, not the element in the list. Keep mutable things as classes, make structs immutable, or index into an array and replace the element with a new value.

ideas.idea: Nullable reference types are compile-time annotations and warnings only; at runtime a string can still be null, so guard values that cross a boundary.
ideas.why: Code that trusts 'string' over 'string?' crashes on JSON, database rows or callers compiled without the feature, which never went through the checker.
ideas.prompt: A DTO property is declared `public string Email { get; set; }` with nullable enabled, and the code never checks it. A client posts JSON without email and the service throws NullReferenceException. Why did the compiler not save you?
ideas.answer: The annotation only tells the compiler what you promise; the deserializer is free to leave the property null, and no runtime check is inserted. Validate at the boundary (required members, model validation or an explicit guard), then inner code can rely on the non-null type honestly.

ideas.idea: Compare identifiers, keys and protocol text with ordinal comparison; culture-aware comparison and formatting are for text shown to people.
ideas.why: Culture rules change results by machine locale: a case-insensitive check can fail on a Turkish server, and a number formatted with a comma breaks a parser.
ideas.prompt: A login check does `user.Role.ToUpper() == "ADMIN"` and a price export uses `price.ToString()`. Both pass tests in the US and fail for a customer in Istanbul or Berlin. Explain and fix.
ideas.answer: ToUpper and ToString use the current culture: in Turkish 'i' upper-cases to a dotted capital, and in German the decimal separator is a comma. For identifiers compare with StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase; for machine-readable output format with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture.

ideas.idea: Make a switch expression name every case explicitly; if it needs a discard arm, make that arm throw, never return an ordinary value, so a new case fails loudly.
ideas.why: When someone adds an enum value, a catch-all that maps to a normal result silently does the wrong thing instead of failing a build or a test.
ideas.prompt: An enum of call results gains a new member, RateLimited. The mapper from results to HTTP status codes ends with `_ => 200` and still compiles, so rate-limited calls now return 200. How should the mapper have been written?
ideas.answer: Name every member in its own arm. Without a catch-all, adding RateLimited makes the compiler warn that the switch is not exhaustive (CS8509), and warnings-as-errors stops the build. If a discard is kept for unnamed enum values, it throws, so the missing case fails in the first test instead of returning 200.

ideas.idea: Records compare by value and support non-destructive change with `with`; the copy is shallow, so collection members are still shared.
ideas.why: Classes used as value objects compare by reference, so two equal amounts are 'different', and a with-copy that shares a mutable list leaks changes back.
ideas.prompt: `var b = a with { Total = 0 };` is meant to produce an independent cart, but adding to b.Lines also changes a.Lines. Both are records. Explain, and say when records are the right choice.
ideas.answer: with copies the record's fields, and Lines is a reference to the same list, so both carts share it. Use immutable collections inside records, or copy the list explicitly in the with expression. Records fit values that are defined by their data, such as money or an email address, where equal contents should mean equal objects.

ideas.idea: A LINQ query is a recipe that runs each time it is enumerated; materialise it once with ToList when you read it twice or the source may change.
ideas.why: Enumerating twice repeats the work or the database query, and a query read after the source changed returns different results than the ones you checked.
ideas.prompt: `var big = orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100);` is followed by `if (big.Any())` and `foreach (var o in big)`. Against EF Core the log shows two SQL queries, and in memory the loop sometimes sees orders added in between. Explain.
ideas.answer: big is not a list, it is a deferred query, so Any() and foreach each run it from scratch: two round trips, and each sees the source as it is at that moment. Call ToList() once when the results should be one consistent snapshot, then test and loop over that list.

ideas.idea: Go async all the way: await instead of .Result or .Wait(), and pass the CancellationToken down to every call that accepts one.
ideas.why: Blocking on a task wastes a thread and can deadlock, and calls without the token keep working after the client has gone away.
ideas.prompt: Under load an ASP.NET Core service's response times explode while CPU stays low, and requests cancelled by the client keep running queries for seconds. The code calls `client.GetAsync(url).Result` and ignores the token. What do you change?
ideas.answer: Make the method async and await GetAsync, so the thread returns to the pool while the call waits; .Result blocks a thread per request and starves the pool. Accept the request's CancellationToken and pass it to every async call, so cancelled requests stop their HTTP and database work.

ideas.idea: Override Equals and GetHashCode together over the same fields, and keep those fields immutable while the object sits in a hashed collection.
ideas.why: Equal objects with different hash codes are never found in a dictionary or set, and a key mutated after insertion is lost inside it.
ideas.prompt: An Email value object overrides Equals to compare case-insensitively but not GetHashCode. A HashSet<Email> ends up with both 'A@x.com' and 'a@x.com'. Explain and fix.
ideas.answer: HashSet looks in the bucket picked by GetHashCode before it ever calls Equals, and the default hash differs for the two instances, so they never meet. Compute the hash from the same normalised value Equals compares, for example the lower-cased address, or normalise once in the constructor.

ideas.idea: Wrap anything that owns a handle (files, connections, streams, timers) in using, so it is released on every path, exceptions included.
ideas.why: Handles freed only by the garbage collector run out under load: open files, pooled connections and sockets leak long before memory does.
ideas.prompt: A report job opens a FileStream and a SqlConnection, and on certain bad rows it throws before calling Close. After a few hours the database refuses new connections. What is the fix, and why does GC not help?
ideas.answer: Declare both with using (or using statements), so Dispose runs when the scope ends whether it ends normally or by an exception, returning the connection to the pool and closing the file. The garbage collector only runs when memory is short, and nothing forces it to finalise connections before the pool is exhausted.

ideas.idea: On hot paths, measure allocations and use Span<T> or ReadOnlySpan<char> to slice and parse without copying; elsewhere, prefer the clear code.
ideas.why: Substring and Split in a tight loop allocate on every call, so garbage collection pauses grow with traffic, while premature span code in cold paths only adds risk.
ideas.prompt: A log parser handling 200,000 lines a second spends a third of its time in garbage collection; it calls line.Split(' ') and Substring for every field. How do you approach it?
ideas.answer: Confirm with an allocation profile that the parser is the hot path. Then parse with ReadOnlySpan<char> slices of the line and the span-based parse methods, which read the characters in place instead of allocating a new string per field. Keep the simple code everywhere the profile does not point.
